text.p: Oil and gas producer Santos Ltd's aggressive production and acquisition programme is being matched by its record commitment to exploration, as the company plans on maintaining high exploration spending through to 2001.

Santos is spending a record A$173 million on exploration in 1997, comprising at least 109 wells, and managing director Ross Adler told Reuters in an interview the company's five year plan "shows very little reduction in exploration effort".
Adler is upbeat about the company's medium-term prospects, with an increasing effort to redirect the company more to oil and opportunities presented through the deregulation of national gas markets.

The company surprised the market with a 40 percent rise in net profit to A$195.1 million in 1996, and its first quarter report, released on Tuesday, showed record results with sales revenue up by 22.5 percent to A$181.3 million and production volume up by 6.8 percent to 9.6 million barrels of oil (boe).

Adler said he believes Santos has the best acreage in offshore Australia, with its recent MIM Ltd, Parker and Parsley and WMC Ltd acquisitions giving exposure to Indonesia and Papua New Guinea and a bigger stake (45 percent) in the East Spar field in Western Australia.

"The company recognises that significant exploration success is what we are trying to achieve because that is where you get the best chance to add value...the real bang to the buck comes if we can have a major discovery in New Guinea or off the WA (Western Australia) coast and that is what we are chasing," he said.

Even excluding the company's stake in the Bayu Undan project in the Timor Gap which is expected to come onstream in the next decade, Adler believes Santos has a very healthy outlook, with the Stag and Elang-Kakatua oilfields on target to commence production in 1998 and oil prices not creating concern.

The company's strategy is focused on offshore exploration and acquisition, a significant build up in its Western Australian business weighted towards exploration, exploration and development in Indonesia and Papua New Guinea, and exploration and acquisitions in the U.K. and U.S.
The company expects to be able to meet its target to push overseas operations from under ten percent to 20 percent of total company production by 2001.
However, Adler said Santos would require exploration success or acquisition to do so, and it had no plans to go beyond these geographic regions.
"We have actually got more opportunities than we have money for which is a new phase for Santos when typically we have had to go out and create our opportunities," he said.

"It is always a dangerous thing to say, but I think, at the moment, a lot of the elements are coming together and what would cap it all off and convince the doubters is if we could make a major exploration success in the next couple of years, it would finish the re-rating of the company," he said.
With the deregulation of the eastern states gas markets, Adler said Santos was not aiming to be dominant but to build on its established base.
However, he believed the company had the best coverage in Australia, with the best infrastructure, gas reserves, and long-term contracts.
The company, he said, did not see threats in BHP Pty Co Ltd, via its Gippsland Basin production, nor in proposals by US oil giant Chevron to pipe gas from Papua New Guinea to northern Queensland.
Santos would welcome the entry by BHP to the New South Wales market and was not convinced the Papua New Guinea proposal would eventuate, he said.

"You cannot ultimately beat people who have got gas close to the market and that is our great protection on the east coast," he said, adding he did not believe the company would have to consider price cuts to secure future contracts.
"There is this thesis that somehow other people will get into the market and they will subsidise customers...I never understood that concept, you have to get a return on your investment," he said.
